title: What to Do When Someone Dies in North Korea: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in North Korea: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for North Korea: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) provides no accessible domestic civil-registry, social-insurance, health, or probate portals to the public abroad, so this guide cites verified international statutory and treaty archives (WIPO Lex, FAOLEX, and HCCH) alongside official foreign consular advisories and protecting-power resources [1] [4] [5] [6]. Because remote digital administration is unavailable, residents and foreign families must coordinate in person through local People's Committees (population registration organs), relevant DPRK diplomatic missions abroad, or designated protecting powers such as the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang [6] [8] [9].

steps.title: Immediate notification, consular outreach, and civil registration
steps.html:
• Domestic population registration: Within the DPRK, death reporting and civil status recording take place exclusively in person through local hospitals or clinics and the civil registration section of the city or county People's Committee where the person resided or passed away; no online registry portal exists outside the country [1] [4].
  • Foreign nationals and emergency consular channels: For foreign visitors or residents, families must immediately notify their home foreign ministry and insurer, as many Western missions (including the British Embassy in Pyongyang) remain closed and the DPRK exercises strict control over consular access [8] [9].
  • Coordinate via Protecting Power where applicable: Where no resident embassy exists, states such as the United States, Canada, Australia, and others rely on the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang as Protecting Power (or consular intermediary) for limited emergency liaison [6] [7] [9].

steps.title: Burial, cremation, repatriation, and diplomatic legalization
steps.html:
• Local handling and border constraints: Official foreign advisories highlight severe transport, border, and diplomatic limits affecting repatriation of remains or personal effects out of North Korea; coordinate directly with local DPRK state protocols through resident diplomatic missions or protecting powers [8] [9].
  • No Hague Apostille (consular legalization only): Per the HCCH status table, the DPRK is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention [5]. Any DPRK death certificate or court document intended for legal use outside the DPRK requires formal diplomatic or consular legalization through DPRK consular authorities and the receiving country's foreign ministry or embassy [5] [8].

steps.title: State social insurance and foreign insurance claims
steps.html:
• Domestic constitutional support: Under Article 72 of the Socialist Constitution of the DPRK, citizens receive state material assistance via domestic social security and state insurance structures managed through workplaces and local People's Committees [3] [4].
  • Foreign nationals and private insurers: Foreign families must rely on home-country life, travel, or medical evacuation insurers and contact UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO Consular Advice) or Global Affairs Canada emergency centers if the family member's nationality falls under their consular care [8] [9] [10].

steps.title: Conflict-of-laws rules for succession and wills
steps.html:
• Verify governing law under the Law on External Civil Relations: Under Articles 45 and 46 of the DPRK Law on External Civil Relations (as amended by Decree No. 251), inheritance of immovable property is governed by the law of the country where the property sits, whereas inheritance of movable property follows the law of domicile of the deceased (or last residence abroad for overseas DPRK citizens) [1] [2].
  • Validity of testaments: Under Article 46, a will or revocation is governed by the testator's law of domicile, and its formal validity is recognized if it satisfies DPRK law, the law where executed, the testator's residence law, or the law where immovable property lies [1].
  • Jurisdiction over declarations of death: Under Article 51 of the Law on External Civil Relations, competent DPRK authorities exercise jurisdiction over formal declarations regarding incompetence, missing persons, or death inside DPRK territory [1].

steps.title: Settle cross-border assets and home-country filings
steps.html:
• Coordinate home-country probate separately: For foreign nationals whose assets sit outside North Korea, coordinate with home-country probate courts on evidentiary standards where legalized DPRK death records are delayed or unobtainable [5] [8] [9].
  • Preserve all diplomatic correspondence: Retain written diplomatic or protecting-power confirmations from the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang or home foreign ministries to substantiate insurance, pension, and estate petitions [6] [8] [9].
